As usual, load the packages
```{r}
library(icorp26)
library(easystats)
library(ggplot2)
```



Assignment 2 asks you to do the following things:

1. get means on outcome variables for *8* groups  
2. Using SPSS or Excel _or R_, graphically display them on 
a well-labeled barchart  


The first thing that you need to do is to decide on your
variables and these fall into two groups:

1. Outcome variables
2. Variables defining groups.


Because Prof. Battle asked you to get the means, the outcome
variables must be appropriate for calculating a mean.
That means that they should be _numeric_ also known as _interval_.
However, it is sometimes okay to treat _ordinal_ variables
as though they are numbers.  This is probably what you will
need to do.

As an example let's use variables from rss7. You need to pick different
variables.


*Make a list of your outcome variables here*


*Make a list of your group variables here*
Note that grouping variables have different numbers of
categories. To get 8 groups you might need between 2 and 
8 variables.



Also note that we have access to _all_ of the RSS data sets.
Use the one that has the variables you are interested in.

```{r}
library(icorp26)
library(easystats)
```

There are many ways to approach this. You can choose one.

One way would be to get the means for all of the 
categories of a variable. 

In rss7 let's say I choose to compare people 
who live in different regions of the country in terms
of the outcome variable `LIF_GENERAL`  which
is an ordinals scale that goes from "Very satisfied" to
"Very dissatisfied".

```{r}

 
datawizard::means_by_group( to_numeric(rss7$LIF_GENERAL), 
                           by = rss7$DEM_REGION) -> summary_by_region

summary_by_region
```

When we make our plot we will also see this clearly.

If you round you can see that the means are all 1.9!

Also in the console try typing `summary_by_region$Category` 
and hit enter.  You will see how this function lets 
you avoid typing all of the labels!!

```{r}
data_groupmeans_bar(summary_by_region)

```
Let's try something more interesting. 

Are home owners more satisfied with life than renters?

```{r}
datawizard::means_by_group(to_numeric(rss7$LIF_GENERAL), 
                           by = rss7$P_HOMEOWN_R ) -> summary_by_homeownership

summary_by_homeownership 

data_groupmeans_bar(summary_by_homeownership) 
```


In this case, we can see that there is a difference
2.07  - 1.82 =  0.25.  So on average, renters
are higher on life satisfaction by about .25. 
Wait, does that make sense? If we look at the rss7
codebook, we can see that Very Satisfied is given 
a 1 and very dissatisfied is given a 4. So 
a higher score means that someone is more dissatisfied.
We can think of it as a life _dissatisfaction_ measure.

So overall renters are more _dissatisfied with life_.
Still, both groups are largely satisied. 

Make sure you look at the variable definitions before you 
make interpretations that could be backwards!


```{r}
data_groupmeans_ci(summary_by_homeownership, 
                   title = "Confidence intervals for life dissatisfaction")

```
```{r}
plot.dw_group_means(summary_by_homeownership)
```

```{r}
plot.dw_group_means(summary_by_homeownership, title = "Life dissatisfaction by owning or renting") +
     ylim(c(1,4))
```


Now you repeat the same kind of analyses but with 
your chosen variables from your chosen data sets.
